items.name: Dr. Martens
clues: A German army doctor who hurt his ankle skiing in 1945.
Bavaria first. Later, a family shoe company in the English Midlands made them famous.
Normal boots hurt his foot, so he designed a shoe with a soft sole full of air.
The most famous boot is named after the day it was launched: 1 April 1960.
Yellow stitching around the sole, and a loop at the back of the heel.
The founder’s surname (in English spelling), with ‘Dr.’ in front.

items.name: adidas
clues: A shoemaker who started making sports shoes in his mother’s laundry room in the 1920s.
A small town in Franconia. His brother started a rival brand in the same town, and they never made up.
Jesse Owens wore his shoes when he won four gold medals at the 1936 Olympics in Berlin.
Football boots with screw-in studs, worn by West Germany when they won the 1954 World Cup.
Three stripes.
The founder’s nickname, Adi, plus the first three letters of his surname.

items.name: Nike
clues: A university running coach and one of his former runners, in the 1960s.
Oregon, in the north-west of the USA.
At first they imported Japanese running shoes and sold them from a car at athletics events.
The coach poured rubber into his wife’s waffle iron to make a new kind of sole.
A logo like a tick, designed by a student in 1971 for $35.
Named after the Greek goddess of victory.

items.name: Nutella
clues: A pastry maker in northern Italy, just after the Second World War.
Alba, in Piedmont, a region famous for its hazelnuts.
Chocolate was very expensive after the war, so he mixed it with lots of hazelnuts to make it go further.
The first version was a solid block that you cut with a knife. Later it became soft enough to spread.
A glass jar with a white lid, and on the label a slice of bread covered in the spread, with some hazelnuts.
An English word for what hazelnuts are, plus a sweet Italian-sounding ending.

items.name: Louis Vuitton
clues: A teenager who walked from the French mountains to Paris in the 1830s to find work.
Paris, where he packed luggage for rich travellers before opening his own shop in 1854.
His trunks had flat tops, so they could be stacked on trains and ships. Round-topped trunks couldn’t.
Luxury suitcases and handbags. Some of them cost more than a small car.
A brown pattern of initials and flowers, created in 1896 by the founder’s son to stop people copying the bags.
Two initials, L and V.

items.name: Converse
clues: A businessman in Massachusetts who started a rubber shoe company in 1908.
Near Boston, in the north-east of the USA.
It made a basketball shoe in 1917, and a basketball player who sold the shoes later got his name on them.
Canvas trainers with a rubber toe, high-top or low.
A round star on a patch on the ankle.
The founder’s surname, which is also a word for having a conversation. Many people call the shoes ‘Chucks’.
